q: What does the diode inside the Silvia's vibratory pump do?
a: Passes one half of each mains cycle, so each gives one stroke
Stops water flowing back from the boiler into the pump
Cuts power to the pump if the coil overheats
Steps the mains voltage down for the pump coil
why: On each pulse the coil pulls the piston and a spring pushes it back, so the pump strokes at mains frequency: 60 times a second on 60 Hz, 50 on 50 Hz. Check valves stop backflow, and some Silvias have a separate thermal fuse for overheating.

q: What is the Silvia's earth connection for?
a: Giving fault current a path so the protection trips
Carrying the element's return current to the plug
Providing the low-voltage ground for the PCB
Carrying current for the lamps in the rockers
why: Earth bonds the frame, boiler and valve body and carries no current in normal use; neutral is the return. If a live wire touches metal, earth lets the GFCI, RCD or breaker trip instead of leaving the case live. It must never connect to the PCB's low-voltage ground.

q: A vibratory pump can't be slowed down like a motor. How does the PCB control it?

It lowers the voltage to the pump coil smoothly
It changes the frequency of the mains supply
It opens and closes the OPV to bleed pressure
why: Every stroke is a fixed squirt, so the PCB controls how many happen. A zero-cross detector marks each mains cycle and the STM32 decides whether to fire the pump's triac: asking for 50% lets every other cycle through. This is pulse skip modulation, PSM.

Feeds 3.3 V from the switch into the PCB

q: How do the optional hardware scales weigh the shot?

A ToF sensor measuring the level in the cup
The pressure sensor's reading summed over the shot
A strain gauge built into the portafilter handle
